truefeedback.text: Cumulative Frequencies

Worked Solution:

To find the cumulative frequencies we simply add all the frequencies up to and including that of the class interval in question. So, the cumulative frequency at the first class interval is simply the first frequency, namely {@count_1@}. The cumulative frequency at the second interval is \({@count_1@}+{@count_2@} = {@cum_freq_2@}\). Similarly, at the third interval, it is \({@count_1@}+{@count_2@}+{@count_3@} = {@cum_freq_3@}\), and at the fourth it is \({@count_1@}+{@count_2@}+{@count_3@}+{@count_4@} = {@cum_freq_4@}\).
Midpoints

When calculating the midpoint for the first class interval, it seems that you have used {@max1-1@} as the upper class boundary. Since weights are continuous data, we use {@max1@} as the upper class boundary for the second interval. (Remember, weights of {@float(max1-0.4)@} and {@float(max1-0.05)@} would still be included in that interval). Therefore the midpoint should be \(\frac{{@min1@}+{@max1@}}{2} = {@float(midpoint_1)@}\).

When calculating the midpoint for the second class interval, it seems that you have used {@max2-1@} as the upper class boundary. Since weights are continuous data, we use {@max2@} as the upper class boundary for the second interval. (Remember, weights of {@float(max2-0.4)@} and {@float(max2-0.05)@} would still be included in that interval). Therefore the midpoint should be \(\frac{{@min2@}+{@max2@}}{2} = {@float(midpoint_2)@}\).

When calculating the midpoint for the third class interval, it seems that you have used {@max3-1@} as the upper class boundary. Since weights are continuous data, we use {@max3@} as the upper class boundary for the second interval. (Remember, weights of {@float(max3-0.4)@} and {@float(max3-0.05)@} would still be included in that interval). Therefore the midpoint should be \(\frac{{@min3@}+{@max3@}}{2} = {@float(midpoint_3)@}\).

When calculating the midpoint for the fourth class interval, it seems that you have used {@max4-1@} as the upper class boundary. Since weights are continuous data, we use {@max4@} as the upper class boundary for the second interval. (Remember, weights of {@float(max4-0.4)@} and {@float(max4-0.05)@} would still be included in that interval). Therefore the midpoint should be \(\frac{{@min4@}+{@max4@}}{2} = {@float(midpoint_4)@}\).

Worked Solution:

To find the midpoint of a class interval we need to add the minimum and maximum values and divide by 2. In the first interval this would be \(\frac{{@min1@}+{@max1@}}{2} = {@if integerp(midpoint_1) then midpoint_1 else float(midpoint_1)@}\). In the second interval this would be \(\frac{{@min2@}+{@max2@}}{2} = {@if integerp(midpoint_2) then midpoint_2 else float(midpoint_2)@}\). In the third interval this would be \(\frac{{@min3@}+{@max3@}}{2} = {@if integerp(midpoint_3) then midpoint_3 else float(midpoint_3)@}\). In the fourth interval this would be \(\frac{{@min4@}+{@max4@}}{2} = {@if integerp(midpoint_4) then midpoint_4 else float(midpoint_4)@}\).
Midpoints \(\times \) Frequencies
Your answer is not correct but is consistent with your midpoints, which unfortunately are not correct.

Worked Solution:

Here we simply need to multiply the Frequency in each class interval by the respective Midpoint. In the first interval, this would be \({@count_1@}\times {@if integerp(midpoint_1) then midpoint_1 else float(midpoint_1)@} = {@if integerp(estimated_subtotal_1) then estimated_subtotal_1 else float(estimated_subtotal_1)@}\). In the second interval, this would be \({@count_2@}\times {@if integerp(midpoint_2) then midpoint_2 else float(midpoint_2)@} = {@if integerp(estimated_subtotal_2) then estimated_subtotal_2 else float(estimated_subtotal_2)@}\). In the third interval, this would be \({@count_3@}\times {@if integerp(midpoint_3) then midpoint_3 else float(midpoint_3)@} = {@if integerp(estimated_subtotal_3) then estimated_subtotal_3 else float(estimated_subtotal_3)@}\). In the fourth interval, this would be \({@count_4@}\times {@if integerp(midpoint_4) then midpoint_4 else float(midpoint_4)@} = {@if integerp(estimated_subtotal_4) then estimated_subtotal_4 else float(estimated_subtotal_4)@}\).
You multiplied the midpoints by the cumulative frequencies instead of the frequencies.

Worked Solution:

To estimate the value of the mean we consider the estimated total weight calculated in the table and the total number of {@sport_choice@} players. The estimated total weight is {@total_weight@} and the number of players is {@n@}. So a reasonable estimate for the mean would be \(\frac{{@if integerp(total_weight) then total_weight else float(total_weight)@}}{{@n@}} = {@if integerp(estimate_mean) then estimate_mean else dispdp(estimate_mean,1)@}\) {@if integerp(estimate_mean) then "" else "(1 d.p.)"@}.

Note: As the data is presented in a frequency table, we don't know what the original weight of the players was and we can only calculate an estimate of the mean weight. Worked Solution:

The median is the middle element when the elements are ordered from smallest to largest. As the data is given in a frequency table, we can only figure out the class interval where the median value lies. As there are {@n@} {@sport_choice@} players, we need to find where the 'middle' one would be, which would be the one in position number {@ceiling(n/2)@} as there would be {@ceiling(n/2)-1@} players on either side. Looking at the cumulative frequencies we can see this would be in the {@if class_interval_median=1 then "first" elseif class_interval_median=2 then "second" elseif class_interval_median=3 then "third" else "fourth"@} class interval.
